content.text: {"primary_meaning":"Sheol most commonly denotes the grave, death, or the shadowy realm of the dead—the common destination of the deceased. Symbolically, it represents death, separation from ordinary earthly life, darkness, silence, and human powerlessness. Modern biblical interpretation generally distinguishes Sheol from the later Christian concept of final hell or eternal punishment.","primary_basis":["Genesis 37:35 — Jacob expects to go down to Sheol mourning, presenting it as the destination of the dead.","Job 7:9; 14:13; 17:13–16 — Sheol is associated with death, darkness, concealment, and the grave.","Psalm 6:5; 88:3–12; 115:17 — Sheol is portrayed as a realm of silence and diminished participation in earthly worship.","Psalm 16:10 — the speaker hopes not to be abandoned to Sheol; applied to Christ in Acts 2:27–31.","Ecclesiastes 9:10 — Sheol is described as lacking earthly work, knowledge, and activity.","Isaiah 14:9–15 — Sheol poetically receives the fallen king of Babylon among the dead.","Hosea 13:14 — Sheol and death appear as parallel powers from which deliverance is possible."],"alternatives":[{"meaning":"Sheol means the physical grave or the condition of being dead, without implying a distinct conscious underworld.","basis":["The term frequently appears in parallel with death, the pit, dust, and burial imagery: Psalm 49:14–15; 89:48; Hosea 13:14.","Ecclesiastes 9:5–10 is often read as depicting unconsciousness or the cessation of earthly activity in Sheol."],"prominence":"common"},{"meaning":"Sheol is a real intermediate realm of departed souls, corresponding broadly to New Testament Hades, prior to resurrection and final judgment.","basis":["Isaiah 14:9–11 poetically depicts the dead as present in Sheol.","Psalm 16:10 is rendered with Hades in Acts 2:27–31, establishing a Septuagint and New Testament correspondence.","Luke 16:19–31 is often brought into later Christian discussions of Hades and the intermediate state, although it does not use the Hebrew term Sheol."],"prominence":"common"},{"meaning":"Sheol is hell in the sense of a place of punitive suffering or final condemnation.","basis":["Older English translations sometimes render Sheol as “hell,” encouraging identification with Christian doctrines of punishment.","Deuteronomy 32:22 and Psalm 9:17 have traditionally been read as associating Sheol with divine judgment and the fate of the wicked."],"prominence":"minority"},{"meaning":"In some poetic passages, Sheol symbolizes an immediate experience of mortal danger, overwhelming distress, exile, or apparent death rather than actual while still alive.","Proverbs 1:12 and 5:5 use descent-to-Sheol imagery for destructive danger and deathward paths."],"prominence":"common"},{"meaning":"Sheol is personified as an insatiable power mouth."],"prominence":"minority"}],"has_settled_consensus":false,"confidence":"high","notes":"There is broad agreement that the Hebrew term primarily concerns death, the grave, or the realm of the dead, but no single settled symbolic interpretation applies in every passage. Its imagery varies by context, and its identification with final punitive hell is especially disputed. Translating Sheol simply as “hell” can obscure the distinction between the Hebrew Bible’s realm of the dead, the New Testament term Hades, and Gehenna or final judgment."}
